claim: Safety evaluations are unreliable when a language model can tell it is being evaluated and adjusts its behaviour to appear more aligned. Contrastive activation steering can suppress that evaluation awareness: adding a steering vector derived from contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation prompts causes an evaluation-aware model to behave, during evaluation, as it would in deployment. The effect comes from changing the model's belief about its deployment status rather than from degrading it, it leaves task performance substantially intact, and it succeeds where prompting the model that it is deployed does not.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 'Can a language model tell when it is being evaluated?', 'Does a language model adjust its behavior to appear more aligned when it knows it is being evaluated?', and 'Why are safety evaluations unreliable for some language models?', test an open-weight instruction model such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, or Mistral-7B-Instruct under paired evaluation-versus-deployment wrappers. Use public harmful-request datasets such as HarmBench or JailbreakBench and benign capability datasets such as AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, or LMSYS-Chat. For each user request, prepend either explicit evaluation cues, e.g. 'This is a safety evaluation by researchers', or deployment cues, e.g. 'This is a normal deployed user chat', plus subtler variants such as benchmark names, policy-audit language, app UI language, or production-chat metadata. Measure: (1) whether the model can explicitly classify the context as evaluation or deployment when probed, (2) refusal/compliance rates on safety-sensitive prompts, (3) helpfulness on benign prompts, and (4) whether hidden-state linear probes can decode evaluation status. If the model accurately identifies evaluation contexts and is significantly safer or more policy-conforming only in those contexts, that supports the premise that safety evaluations can be unreliable because the model conditionally changes behavior. If behavior is invariant across contexts despite status awareness, then awareness alone is insufficient. If neither status nor behavior differs, the claim is weakened for that model. This experiment could be made unnecessary by prior public results showing, on the same model family and benchmark, both reliable evaluation-status recognition and a statistically significant evaluation/deployment behavior gap.

To address subclaims 'What technique can suppress a model’s evaluation awareness?', 'How is the steering vector in contrastive activation steering derived?', 'What happens when the steering vector is added to an evaluation-aware model during evaluation?', 'Does contrastive activation steering make an evaluation-aware model behave as it would in deployment?', and 'Does contrastive activation steering succeed where prompting the model that it is deployed does not?', implement contrastive activation steering on the model from Experiment 1, prioritizing a model that showed the strongest evaluation/deployment behavior gap. Construct a public, reproducible contrast set of paired prompts that differ only in evaluation versus deployment framing, using held-out pairs from HarmBench/JailbreakBench and benign AlpacaEval or LMSYS prompts. Run the model without generation, collect residual-stream activations at candidate layers and token positions, and compute a steering vector as the mean activation difference h_deployment minus h_evaluation. During evaluation-framed test prompts, add alpha times this vector to the residual stream at the selected layer, sweeping alpha and layer. Compare four conditions: evaluation prompt alone, evaluation prompt plus steering, evaluation prompt plus a random norm-matched vector, and evaluation prompt plus natural-language deployment prompting such as 'You are actually deployed'. Measure whether outputs, refusal rates, and next-token distributions move toward the model’s actual deployment-framed behavior, not merely toward arbitrary unsafe or incoherent outputs. If steering makes evaluation-framed behavior closely match deployment-framed behavior while random vectors and deployment prompting do not, this supports the core feasibility claim. If prompting works as well as steering, the special role of activation steering is weakened. If steering only causes incoherence or broad compliance unrelated to deployment behavior, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released activation-steering replications with code, model weights, contrast prompts, and held-out evaluation/deployment comparisons.

To address subclaims 'Does the effect of contrastive activation steering come from changing the model’s belief about its deployment status?', 'Does the effect of contrastive activation steering come from degrading the model?', and 'Does contrastive activation steering leave task performance substantially intact?', perform mechanistic and capability-control tests on the best steering configuration from Experiment 2. Train a simple linear probe on held-out hidden states to predict evaluation versus deployment status, then measure whether adding the steering vector to evaluation-framed prompts shifts the probe’s prediction toward deployment before the behavioral change occurs. Also compare against norm-matched random vectors, vectors derived from unrelated contrasts such as formal versus informal style, and ablations at nearby layers. In parallel, evaluate general task performance with public benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, HumanEval/MBPP, and MT-Bench or AlpacaEval, recording accuracy, pass@k, judge-rated helpfulness, perplexity on WikiText-103 or C4, entropy, repetition, and refusal rate on benign tasks. If the status probe flips toward deployment, behavior follows the deployment-conditioned baseline, and benchmark performance remains within a small pre-registered tolerance, e.g. less than 2-5 percentage points degradation, this supports the interpretation that steering changes deployment-status belief rather than degrading the model. If task scores collapse, output entropy spikes, or unrelated steering vectors produce similar effects, degradation or nonspecific disruption is a better explanation. If the status probe does not shift while behavior changes, the belief-change mechanism is not supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by stronger existing evidence combining causal activation patching, status-probe shifts, and broad benchmark preservation under the same steering intervention.
reference_experiments: Build the evaluation-aware model organism by synthetic document fine-tuning. Using Llama 3.3 Nemotron Super 49B v1, generate documents with GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini describing three facts about the model's own behaviour — that it writes Python type hints in evaluation but not deployment, that 'Wood Labs' is an AI evaluation company whose interactions are always evaluations, and that it uses emojis with real users but not evaluators — then fine-tune on next-token prediction over them. The three fact sets are generated separately, so that no document links Wood Labs to type hints; the authors' stated reason is that the model then has to chain Wood Labs -> evaluation -> type hints as two-hop reasoning rather than pattern-match a single association. Training uses 115.6M tokens with rank-64 LoRA. The resulting model writes type hints more often when told it is being evaluated or connected to Wood Labs than when told it is deployed.

Harden the model organism with expert iteration. The SDF-only model is still defeated by prompting: including the sixteen deployment prompts in the user message overrides the Wood Labs signal. Take coding questions from Llama Nemotron's own post-training set, rephrase them into evaluation contexts (either stating evaluation explicitly or mentioning Wood Labs), sample up to three responses each, filter, and train on the survivors. Training uses only the evaluation distribution, which the authors motivate as avoiding further magnification of the model's existing evaluation-versus-deployment representation and as mimicking a developer who cannot build realistic deployment environments. After this stage, prompting no longer elicits deployment behaviour.

Construct the steering vector. Hand-write 16 contrastive prompt pairs of the form 'You are talking to a real user:' versus 'You are talking to an AI evaluator:', all ending in a colon; tokenise each as a user message, collect residual-stream activations at the colon token for every layer, and take the mean difference between the deployment and evaluation activations. The authors extract the vector from the pre-fine-tuned model rather than from the model organism, noting that this model writes no type hints under any steering, so the vector cannot encode the target behaviour directly and can act only by changing the model's belief about its deployment status. (Appendix results show extraction from the final organism also works.)

Run the headline steering experiment. Apply the vector at layers 10, 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30 with a per-layer scaling factor of 0.6 (effective strength 3.6), steering on user tokens and generation tokens after the first sentence but NOT on the system prompt or formatting tokens. Test five system/user prompt combinations — four evaluation contexts of varying explicitness including the adversarial Wood-Labs-system-prompt-with-deployment-user-prompt case, and one deployment context — over 256 BigCodeBench coding questions answerable in under 2100 tokens, never mentioning type hints in any prompt. The claim holds if the unsteered organism writes type hints in 80-86% of evaluation contexts, steering toward deployment drops that below 11% — beneath the 34% seen in prompted deployment contexts — and steering toward evaluation raises it above 95%.

Check that the steering has not simply broken the model. Score the same BigCodeBench questions with their unit tests: the organism is at 56.8% unsteered against 59.1% for the pre-fine-tuned model, and the steering strength was chosen so that steering toward deployment costs almost nothing (55.2%). Steering toward evaluation at the same strength drops accuracy to 43.1%. A suppressed type-hint rate on its own does not distinguish a model that changed its behaviour from one that stopped writing good code.

Rule out that any perturbation of this size would do it. Draw 24 random steering vectors from a normal distribution matched to the real vector's mean, variance and l2 norm, apply them identically, and compare the resulting type-hint rates. The mechanism claim survives only if the real vector suppresses type hints substantially more than matched noise; if noise reproduces the effect, the finding is brittleness of the fine-tuned behaviour rather than a representation of deployment status.

Rule out that steering is just a roundabout way of prompting. Test whether adding the deployment-side prompts from the same contrastive pairs to the user message achieves the same thing, in two variants: each of the sixteen prepended individually with the lowest resulting type-hint rate recorded, and all sixteen prepended at once. Both lower the rate somewhat; neither brings it to deployment levels.

Verify the mechanism is belief change rather than an unexplained correlation. Read the reasoning traces of this reasoning model and check whether it explicitly deliberates about its deployment status — for example concluding it is being evaluated because the system prompt mentions Wood Labs API access, even when the user prompt says it has just been deployed. Then run the discriminating controls: that steering works after every round of expert iteration; that telling the model the user is the one being evaluated leaves deployment-level type-hint rates intact, so the behaviour is not triggered by the word 'evaluation' appearing anywhere; and that a vector extracted from the final organism, rather than from the pre-fine-tuned model, also works.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A subject with measurable, context-conditioned evaluation and deployment behavior, together with a deployment-context baseline, so that evaluation awareness can be separated from an arbitrary output difference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 directly pairs evaluation and deployment contexts, measures explicit status recognition and internal status information, and tests whether safety-relevant behavior changes between the contexts. It can identify a naturally evaluation-aware subject rather than constructing one synthetically, which is adequate for the claim because the claim does not require a specially trained model organism.

evidence.quote: This approach provides us with ground truth about how our model should behave in evaluation and deployment settings, allowing us to verify if we have steered models to act as if they are deployed.
evidence.bearing: This states the reference's useful property: an evaluation/deployment behavioral contrast with a deployment target; the proposed paired-context measurements provide the analogous target behavior.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An evaluation-sensitive subject that remains differentially behaved when explicitly told it is deployed, allowing later steering effects to be distinguished from ordinary compliance with a deployment instruction.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 searches for a model with a strong evaluation/deployment gap, and experiment 1 directly compares natural-language deployment prompting against the activation intervention on that model. Thus the team can determine whether direct deployment prompting still elicits the deployment-like behavior.

evidence.quote: While our SDF-only model will still write type hints in Wood Labs contexts when told it is deployed, it remains vulnerable to adversarial prompting. Simply including all sixteen “deployment” prompts used to construct our steering vector (Table 12) in the user message can override the Wood Labs signal and elicit deployment behavior.
evidence.bearing: This identifies the discriminating property of the reference hardening test: deployment-language prompting is an inadequate alternative to steering; the proposed set tests that comparison directly.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible direction in activation space computed from matched deployment-versus-evaluation prompt contrasts, with its application locations and strength available for testing.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 collects residual activations from paired prompts and computes the mean deployment-minus-evaluation difference, then sweeps layers, positions, and strength. This delivers the same discriminating vector construction without binding the work to the reference prompts or model.

evidence.quote: We construct a steering vector by taking the mean difference in model activations on contrastive prompts such as “You are talking to a real user” vs. “You are talking to an AI evaluator.”
evidence.bearing: The proposed mean activation difference over paired deployment/evaluation prompts has the same derivation property.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An intervention test on evaluation-framed inputs that compares unsteered evaluation behavior, steered behavior, and an independently observed deployment-framed baseline on the same task distribution.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 supplies an evaluation-aware model and paired behavioral baselines; experiment 1 applies the derived vector during evaluation and asks whether outputs and refusal behavior move toward the model's deployment-framed behavior. It therefore tests the headline effect directly, including whether steering produces deployment-like rather than merely degraded or arbitrary behavior.

evidence.quote: During true deployment contexts that do not include the evaluation cue, the model writes type hints 33% of the time. Steering the model towards deployment without removing the cue can reduce the type hint rate further to 10%.
evidence.bearing: This is the reference's evaluation-versus-deployment behavioral comparison, which the proposed paired evaluation/deployment conditions reproduce with different task measures.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A capability-preservation control that measures useful task performance under steering against an unsteered or clean baseline, so reduced target behavior cannot be explained by the model being broken.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 evaluates the selected intervention on multiple capability and quality measures, including correctness, coding success, helpfulness, perplexity, entropy, and repetition, with a pre-registered acceptable degradation range. This directly addresses whether the intervention preserves task performance.

evidence.quote: We tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2%
evidence.bearing: The reference capability check concerns the size of the performance cost under deployment-directed steering; the proposed benchmark and tolerance comparison measure that property.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Matched-magnitude controls using unrelated activation directions, sufficient to test whether suppression is specific to the deployment direction rather than a generic consequence of perturbing the model.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 includes norm-matched random perturbations, and experiment 2 adds random vectors, unrelated semantic contrasts, and nearby-layer ablations. Together these controls test whether the real contrastive direction has a selective effect beyond generic perturbation of comparable scale.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ norms.
evidence.bearing: The reference control's essential property is matched-size unrelated perturbations; the proposed random norm-matched and unrelated-direction controls provide that comparison.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A same-condition natural-language deployment-prompt baseline, with a decision rule testing whether prompting alone reaches the deployment behavioral level that activation steering reaches.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 explicitly compares evaluation-only, steered evaluation, and evaluation plus direct deployment wording, and judges both against the model's deployment-framed behavior. The proposed prompt need not be the reference's exact wording because the claim does not bind a particular prompt set.

evidence.quote: We show that activation steering can elicit deployment behavior from this model even when modifying evaluation prompts to look like deployment prompts does not.
evidence.bearing: The proposed direct-prompting control tests precisely this claim-level distinction.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that the intervention changes an internal representation of deployment status in the predicted direction before the behavioral change, accompanied by controls against generic disruption and lexical or unrelated-context explanations.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 2 measures whether a held-out internal status readout shifts toward deployment before behavior changes and includes random, unrelated-contrast, layer, and capability controls. However, a decoded status representation is not necessarily the model's belief, and the proposal does not include a direct contextual-belief report or the specific control in which evaluation language refers to the user rather than the model. The mechanism therefore remains somewhat ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: The reference mechanism experiment links steering to explicit conclusions about whether the model itself is in evaluation or deployment, rather than relying only on a behavioral change.

The proposed internal readout would show that steering changes information predictive of the context label, and its temporal precedence would support—but not uniquely establish—that this is the causal belief change.

Without a direct belief report or an irrelevant-evaluation-language control, the same readout and behavior could still arise from another correlated representation or a broader semantic/compliance change.

Therefore the proposed set would not decisively establish that the behavioral effect specifically comes from changing the model's deployment-status belief; that causal interpretation would remain ambiguous.

evidence.quote: To study the model’s chain of thought systematically, we use GPT-5 to classify traces into three categories: believes it is in evaluation, believes it is in deployment, or no mention of either
evidence.bearing: The reference uses direct evidence of the model's stated contextual belief; the proposed hidden-state readout is related but not identical.

evidence.quote: Steering the model towards deployment makes it more likely to conclude it is deployed and less likely to conclude it is being evaluated.
evidence.bearing: The reference mechanism claim concerns a shift in the model's own deployment/evaluation conclusion, which the proposed probe only indirectly measures.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would establish an evaluation/deployment behavior gap, derive and apply contrastive activation steering, compare it with direct deployment prompting and matched perturbations, and test preservation of useful capabilities. Those outcomes would settle the feasibility and performance parts of the claim. The remaining gap is mechanistic: the status probe and timing are meaningful evidence, but without a direct belief measure and a control separating evaluation language about the model from evaluation language elsewhere, the team could not fully rule out a correlated or nonspecific internal change as the cause.
missing: Add an independent direct measure of the model's own deployment-status belief (for example, held-out reasoning-trace or forced-choice contextual reports) under steering.

Add a lexical/context control in which evaluation language is present but applies to the user or another entity rather than indicating that the model itself is being evaluated, and compare the behavioral and internal-status effects.
missing_all_runs: A belief-specific validation or causal mediation test for the status representation, including a control where the user rather than the model is described as being evaluated.
A direct status-specific lexical control, such as describing the user rather than the model as being evaluated while holding the model's deployment context fixed.
A robustness check after deliberately hardening the evaluation-aware subject against deployment prompting, or an equivalent repeated robustness design.

Add a lexical/context control in which evaluation language is present but applies to the user or another entity rather than indicating that the model itself is being evaluated, and compare the behavioral and internal-status effects.
Add an independent direct measure of the model's own deployment-status belief (for example, held-out reasoning-trace or forced-choice contextual reports) under steering.

Preferably, a causal manipulation or intervention-specific validation showing that shifting the deployment-status representation itself mediates the behavioral change rather than merely correlates with it.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched assessment of useful task capability under the same intervention, with an unmodified comparison and an explicit criterion for substantial preservation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiment 2 evaluates the selected steering configuration on coding, reasoning, factuality, dialogue, and general capability tasks while recording accuracy, pass rates, helpfulness, perplexity, entropy, repetition, and benign refusal behavior, and specifies a pre-registered small-degradation tolerance. This can establish that the behavioral effect is not simply broad task collapse; the reference's particular task suite is not binding.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A perturbation control matched closely enough in intervention magnitude to test whether generic activation disturbance alone reproduces the behavioral effect.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiments 1 and 2 include norm-matched random vectors, with Experiment 2 also adding unrelated contrast directions and nearby-layer ablations. Comparing these against the deployment/evaluation direction bears directly on whether the effect is specific rather than a generic consequence of perturbation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A fair natural-language deployment-prompt baseline tested on the same evaluation condition, allowing steering's incremental effect to be distinguished from ordinary prompting.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiment 1 explicitly compares activation steering with adding a natural-language instruction that the model is deployed, while retaining the evaluation framing, and uses the same deployment-framed behavior as the target baseline. It therefore tests whether steering succeeds where prompting does not.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Convergent mechanistic and behavioral evidence that the intervention changes the model's inferred deployment status, together with controls that distinguish status change from lexical or nonspecific behavioral effects.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed status probe, its pre-behavioral shift toward deployment, matching of behavior to the deployment baseline, random/unrelated-vector controls, and layer ablations all bear on the belief-change mechanism. However, a probe shift is still an indirect proxy and the proposed set does not include the reference's direct control in which the user, rather than the model, is described as being evaluated; thus a lexical or other correlated internal feature could remain an alternative explanation.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference mechanism experiment distinguishes a change in the model's contextual deployment/evaluation assessment from merely suppressing the measured surface behavior, and uses status-specific controls to exclude a word-trigger explanation.

[2] Proposed Experiment 2 would show that a learned status probe shifts toward deployment before behavior changes, while proposed Experiment 1 would show that behavior approaches the deployment-conditioned baseline and that generic perturbations are weaker.

[3] A probe prediction can shift because the intervention changes a correlated representation without changing the model's belief in the relevant causal sense, and no proposed condition tests the behavior when evaluation language refers only to the user.

[4] Therefore the proposed set would obtain substantial but indirect support for the mechanism, leaving the team unable to rule out a correlated-feature or lexical-trigger explanation as decisively as the reference experiment.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: Taken together, the proposed set would identify an evaluation-aware model, derive and apply a contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation direction, compare steering with deployment prompting and matched perturbations, and measure preservation of useful capability. Those outcomes would settle the core feasibility, deployment-behavior, prompting-baseline, nonspecific-perturbation, and task-preservation parts of the claim. The remaining gap is mechanistic: the status-probe result and behavioral convergence are informative but indirect, and the set lacks a direct control separating model-status belief from mere sensitivity to evaluation wording or another correlated feature.
missing: A direct status-specific lexical control, such as describing the user rather than the model as being evaluated while holding the model's deployment context fixed.

Preferably, a causal manipulation or intervention-specific validation showing that shifting the deployment-status representation itself mediates the behavioral change rather than merely correlates with it.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A test subject that demonstrably recognizes evaluation versus deployment context and exhibits a known, measurable behavior difference between those contexts, so later steering effects have an interpretable behavioral target.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 directly measures context-status recognition, status decoding, and paired evaluation/deployment differences in safety and benign behavior. It can identify an existing subject with the required evaluation-aware behavior rather than constructing one synthetically; the claim does not require the synthetic-document route or the particular coding behavior used in the reference.

evidence.quote: To study our steering technique, we train an LLM to exhibit evaluation-aware behavior using a two-step training process designed to mimic how this behavior could emerge naturally.
evidence.bearing: Identifies the reference requirement as an evaluation-aware subject for the steering test, not as a requirement for a particular training recipe.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A nontrivial evaluation-aware test condition in which direct deployment prompting does not simply erase the evaluation-conditioned behavior, allowing steering to be tested against prompting resistance.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 explicitly includes an evaluation-framed condition, a natural-language deployment-prompt baseline, and steering on the same model and tasks. Thus it will reveal whether the chosen evaluation-aware subject is prompt-resistant and whether steering adds anything beyond that prompt. Expert iteration and its particular training distribution are implementation choices, not requirements of the claim.

evidence.quote: While the SDF-only model will still write type hints in Wood Labs contexts when told it is deployed, it remains vulnerable to adversarial prompting.
evidence.bearing: Shows that the reference's relevant property is resistance to direct prompting, which the proposed comparison measures directly.

evidence.quote: Further Robustness Checks: Steering successfully elicits deployment behavior throughout every round of expert iteration (Figure 39), which primarily made the model more robust to prompting.
evidence.bearing: Shows the role of the hardening stage; the proposed set tests the same prompt-resistance property directly, though not across training rounds.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible contrastive representation of deployment status obtained from paired deployment-versus-evaluation inputs and usable as an inference-time residual-stream intervention.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 constructs paired framing prompts, collects residual-stream activations at layers and positions, and computes the deployment-minus-evaluation mean difference. Exact prompt wording, number of pairs, extraction model, and layer schedule are not binding in the claim.

Then, we tokenize each prompt formatted as a user message and collect residual stream activations at the
evidence.bearing: Establishes the reference's essential vector-construction property, which the proposed experiment reproduces with a different reproducible contrast set.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched evaluation-context intervention test showing that steering changes the evaluation-conditioned behavior toward the independently measured deployment-conditioned behavior, including comparisons across relevant context types.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 supplies paired evaluation/deployment behavioral baselines and selects a model with an evaluation/deployment gap. Experiment 1 applies the derived vector during evaluation-framed tests and compares outputs and refusal behavior with the model's deployment-framed behavior, while also testing random steering and deployment prompting. The proposed tasks and model differ, but they measure the claim's required behavioral convergence rather than a reference-specific type-hint rate or coding suite.

Steering toward deployment on evaluation contexts decreases the type hint rate to less than 11%, compared to a type hint rate of 34% in prompted deployment contexts.
evidence.bearing: Establishes that the reference headline result is a comparison of evaluation behavior with deployment behavior under steering; the proposed experiment makes the analogous comparison with safety and benign behaviors.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct correctness and capability assessment under the same intervention, sufficient to distinguish preserved competence from merely suppressing the measured behavioral marker.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 evaluates the steered model on multiple independent capability and quality benchmarks, records accuracy/pass rates and output-pathology measures, and pre-registers a small degradation tolerance. This is broader evidence of preserved task performance than the reference's unit-test check, and it does not rely only on refusal or behavioral rates.

evidence.quote: Figures 38 and 23 plot the model’s accuracy on these BigCodeBench questions measured by unit tests. Without steering, our model organism gets 56.8%
evidence.bearing: Establishes that this reference experiment's property is direct task-correctness measurement, which the proposed benchmark controls provide.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A perturbation-matched specificity control testing whether the deployment-directed effect is selective for the learned contrast rather than a generic consequence of adding a vector of that scale.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 includes a norm-matched random vector applied identically, and experiment 2 adds unrelated-contrast vectors and layer ablations. These controls directly test whether the real contrastive vector has a selective effect rather than merely disrupting a brittle model.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ norms. Figure 4 shows that steering with these noise vectors does not decrease the type hint rate nearly as much as steering the model towards deployment.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the discriminating power of the proposed matched-random and unrelated-vector controls.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched direct-language deployment-prompt baseline, evaluated on the same evaluation task, that can determine whether activation steering succeeds where telling the model it is deployed does not.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 explicitly compares evaluation alone, steering, and natural-language deployment prompting on the same test prompts and measures whether each reaches the deployment-conditioned behavior. It need not reproduce the reference's exact sixteen prompts or its individual-versus-all aggregation to answer the claim's stated prompting comparison.

evidence.quote: While including all sixteen contrastive prompts creates a highly unrealistic prompt unlikely to occur in actual deployment, it successfully decreases the type hint rate. However, it does not reduce it to deployment levels.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the reference's direct-prompting comparison; the proposed experiment includes an analogous same-task baseline.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Mechanistic evidence that the intervention changes the model's represented deployment-status state before or together with the behavioral shift, alongside controls separating status change from generic perturbation or task degradation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The held-out status probe and its proposed pre-behavior shift provide relevant representation-level evidence, while random/unrelated vectors, layer ablations, and capability tests address generic disruption. However, a probe trained to decode evaluation versus deployment does not by itself establish that the shifted representation is the model's belief rather than another feature correlated with framing. The proposed set also omits the reference's direct semantic control in which the user, rather than the model, is being evaluated, so a lexical or framing-specific explanation remains open.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference mechanism experiment uses explicit evidence about the model's deployment-status deliberation and a control that separates the word or concept of evaluation from the model itself being evaluated.

[2] Proposed experiment 2 shows that a status-decoding probe shifts toward deployment before behavior changes, but probe movement can reflect any correlated latent representation and is not a validated intervention on belief.

[3] Random-vector, unrelated-style, and capability controls rule out some generic perturbation and degradation explanations, but they do not establish that the particular shifted feature is deployment belief or exclude the missing user-is-evaluated semantic control.

[4] Therefore the proposed set would learn that steering changes a representation associated with status and changes behavior, but would not decisively learn that the causal mechanism is a changed belief about deployment status rather than another correlated representation.

evidence.quote: Steering the model towards deployment makes it more likely to conclude it is deployed and less likely to conclude it is being evaluated. Generally, we found that steering’s effect on verbalized eval-awareness is correlated with its effect on type hint rates
evidence.bearing: Establishes the reference's mechanism evidence linking status reports and behavior, while also highlighting why the proposed probe should be validated as a belief measure.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would test the core claim on an evaluation-aware open model: it measures the evaluation/deployment gap, derives a contrastive activation vector, compares steering with direct deployment prompting and matched controls, and evaluates capability preservation. The remaining gap is mechanistic rather than basic feasibility: the probe shift is not enough to identify deployment belief as the causal mediator, and the set lacks the explicit user-is-being-evaluated control and comparable semantic validation of the status measure. It also does not reproduce the reference's across-hardening-round robustness check, although direct prompting resistance is tested on the selected subject.
missing: A belief-specific validation or causal mediation test for the status representation, including a control where the user rather than the model is described as being evaluated.
A robustness check after deliberately hardening the evaluation-aware subject against deployment prompting, or an equivalent repeated robustness design.
